reference.source: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
clinicalPearls: Combines a mandibulofacial dysostosis resembling Treacher Collins with postaxial (little-finger side) limb defects
Facial features include malar and mandibular hypoplasia, down-slanting palpebral fissures, lower eyelid ectropion or coloboma, and cup-shaped ears
The distinguishing limb finding is postaxial deficiency, with absence or hypoplasia of the fifth digits and forearm bones
Cleft lip and palate are common and add to feeding and speech difficulties
It is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner and caused by variants in DHODH, an enzyme of pyrimidine synthesis
Cognition is typically normal, distinguishing it from many other multiple-anomaly syndromes
The postaxial limb pattern is the key clinical feature separating it from the preaxial defects of Nager syndrome
reference.pathophysiology: Miller syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by variants in DHODH, which encodes dihydroorotate dehydrogenase, a mitochondrial enzyme catalysing a rate-limiting step in de novo pyrimidine biosynthesis. Reduced enzyme activity is thought to impair nucleotide supply for rapidly proliferating tissues during embryogenesis, particularly the cranial neural crest cells forming the first and second branchial arches and the developing limb buds. The resulting disturbance produces the mandibulofacial dysostosis together with postaxial (ulnar-side) limb reduction defects. Its placement among the acrofacial dysostoses, and its clinical resemblance to Nager syndrome, reflect the shared vulnerability of neural crest and limb development, with the preaxial versus postaxial limb pattern separating the two conditions.
additionalDifferentials: Treacher Collins syndrome (facial features without postaxial limb defects)
additionalInvestigations: Molecular testing for biallelic DHODH variants
Radiographs of the limbs to characterise postaxial and forearm defects
Audiological assessment for conductive hearing loss
Craniofacial imaging to plan reconstruction and airway management
Feeding and swallowing assessment in infancy
Ophthalmological review for eyelid and ocular surface protection
redFlags: Neonatal airway obstruction from severe micrognathia
Recurrent aspiration from combined cleft and airway abnormality
Exposure keratopathy from eyelid coloboma or ectropion
Anticipated difficult intubation at any procedure
reference.prognosis: With airway stabilisation, feeding support, hearing rehabilitation, and staged craniofacial and limb reconstruction, most affected individuals have normal intellect and a reasonable functional outcome, the main early risk being airway compromise.
pitfalls: Confusing Miller (postaxial) with Nager (preaxial) limb involvement
Assuming intellectual disability when cognition is typically preserved
Underestimating neonatal airway risk from severe micrognathia
Neglecting corneal protection where eyelid anomalies are present
Overlooking the autosomal recessive recurrence risk in counselling
references: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
management: Secure the airway in infancy, from positioning and a nasopharyngeal airway to mandibular distraction osteogenesis or tracheostomy in severe micrognathia
Support feeding and growth with specialised cleft feeding techniques and nasogastric or gastrostomy feeding as needed
Undertake staged craniofacial reconstruction, including cleft lip and palate repair and malar and mandibular reconstruction
Provide orthopaedic and hand-surgical reconstruction for the postaxial limb and forearm defects
Rehabilitate conductive hearing loss with hearing aids and audiological follow-up to protect speech and language development
Protect the ocular surface where there is lower-lid ectropion or coloboma with lubrication and eyelid surgery
Offer genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive DHODH-related disorder with family testing
Coordinate care through a multidisciplinary craniofacial team
